# A Representation Bake-Off {#sec-bake-off}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** Every number on this page was produced by
running the code shown, on one machine, with `scikit-learn` 1.9.0,
`gensim` 4.4.0, NumPy 2.5.2 and pandas 3.0.5 on Python 3.12.13. The data is
public and the script is a few hundred lines; you can reproduce all of it in
about four minutes.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- take a real, messy, imbalanced dataset and build the whole pipeline from
  raw text to a scored prediction, using only @sec-text-as-data and
  @sec-embeddings;
- explain why accuracy is the wrong headline number here, and choose macro-F1
  instead — with the arithmetic to show why;
- predict, before running anything, which of the two chapters' methods will
  win on a given problem, and defend the prediction with the *size of the
  labelled set* rather than with the sophistication of the method;
- demonstrate the out-of-vocabulary problem on Turkish and show precisely
  what fastText fixes — and what it clearly does not;
- name the one failure both representation families share, which is the
  reason the rest of this book exists.

## Two chapters, one argument to settle

@sec-text-as-data taught you to count words. @sec-embeddings taught you to
place them as coordinates. Each chapter ended with a claim, and the claims do
not agree.

::: {#gloss-baseline .column-margin .term-gloss}
**baseline** — the plain, cheap method a fancier one has to beat before it
is worth its cost. Reporting a score without one tells the reader nothing. [↩](#term-baseline){.term-back}
:::

::: {#gloss-agglutinative .column-margin .term-gloss}
**agglutinative** — describes a language, like Turkish, that builds
meaning by stacking endings onto a stem. One stem can therefore appear as
hundreds of separate written words. [↩](#term-agglutinative){.term-back}
:::

Chapter 2 said: a sparse count vector is a strong, cheap, interpretable
[baseline](#gloss-baseline){#term-baseline .term-ref} that people routinely fail to beat. Chapter 3 said: one-hot
coordinates cannot generalise across word forms, which for an [agglutinative](#gloss-agglutinative){#term-agglutinative .term-ref}
language like Turkish is a structural defect, not a nuisance — and it
measured 7.33% of Turkish Wikipedia tokens falling outside a
one-million-token vocabulary to prove the point.

Both claims are correct. They are also, on any *particular* dataset,
in direct competition, and the competition is decided by facts about your
data rather than by the merits of the methods. This chapter runs the
competition properly — one dataset, one split, one classifier, seven
representations — and extracts the decision rule.

::: {.column-margin}
Chapter 3's own comparison ran on 20 Newsgroups: English, balanced, four
classes, 2,327 training documents. Every conclusion here that differs from
that one differs because the *dataset* differs, not because the code does.
That is the whole lesson in one sentence.
:::

The setup is deliberately boring. Everything downstream of the
representation is held fixed: the same train/test split, the same
`LogisticRegression`, the same class weighting, the same random seed. The
only thing that varies is how the text becomes numbers. When the scores
differ, the representation is the only thing that can have caused it.

## The problem

**Turkish product reviews, labelled positive or negative.** 235,165 reviews
scraped from a Turkish e-commerce site, distributed as a single parquet file.
Short, informal, unedited: misspellings, missing diacritics, run-together
words, the whole texture of text people actually write.

It is chosen for three reasons, each of which stresses something the previous
chapters claimed.

1. **It is Turkish**, so @sec-embeddings' morphology argument is on trial
   rather than on paper.
2. **It is genuinely imbalanced** — the positive class is fourteen times
   larger — so the metric question cannot be dodged.
3. **It is large enough to subsample**, which lets us ask the question that
   actually decides these things in practice: *how many labels do you have?*

```python
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

URL = ("https://huggingface.co/datasets/turkish_product_reviews/"
       "resolve/main/data/train-00000-of-00001.parquet")
df = pd.read_parquet(URL).rename(
    columns={"sentence": "text", "sentiment": "label"})
df["text"] = df["text"].astype(str).str.strip()
df = df.drop_duplicates(subset="text")
```

```text
### the raw data
rows as downloaded      235,165
after de-duplication    233,508      (1,657 exact duplicates removed)
label 1 (positive)      218,747      93.7%
label 0 (negative)       14,761       6.3%
```

De-duplicate *before* splitting, always. 1,657 duplicates is only 0.7% of the
file, but a duplicate sitting on both sides of the train/test split is a
memorised answer scoring as a generalisation, and it inflates every method
unevenly — whichever model memorises hardest benefits most. This one line
is the difference between an experiment and a demo.

We then take a stratified 50,000-review subsample and split it 80/20,
preserving the imbalance exactly:

```text
### the split (stratified, seed 42)
train    40,000     37,471 positive    2,529 negative
test     10,000      9,368 positive      632 negative
```

::: {.column-margin}
Subsampling to 50,000 is a convenience, not a necessity — it keeps the whole
experiment under four minutes so you can rerun it while reading. The
qualitative conclusions are unchanged on the full 233,508; the sparse methods
gain roughly a point and the dense ones do not.
:::

## The trap in the first number you will compute

Predict "positive" for every review. Never look at the text at all.

```text
### the majority-class baseline
accuracy   93.68%
```

That is the number a stakeholder will hear, and it sounds like a solved
problem. It is a model with no inputs. It has never read a review and never
will, and it is right 93.68% of the time because 93.68% of the test set is
positive.

The failure is invisible in accuracy and glaring the moment you write down
the confusion matrix:

```text
### majority baseline, in full
                   predicted neg   predicted pos
actual neg    632              0             632
actual pos  9,368              0           9,368

precision (neg)   undefined — it never predicts negative
recall    (neg)   0.0%       — it finds none of the 632
F1        (neg)   0.00
F1        (pos)   96.74
macro-F1          48.37
```

**Macro-F1 is the average of the per-class F1 scores**, giving each class
equal weight regardless of size. That single choice is what makes the useless
model look useless: 48.37 instead of 93.68.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why macro-F1, spelled out with the actual arithmetic

For one class, with $TP$ true positives, $FP$ false positives and $FN$ false
negatives:

$$
\text{precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}, \qquad
\text{recall} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}, \qquad
F_1 = \frac{2 \cdot \text{precision} \cdot \text{recall}}{\text{precision} + \text{recall}}
$$

$F_1$ is the *harmonic* mean of precision and recall, and the harmonic mean is
the one that refuses to be bribed. The arithmetic mean of precision 1.00 and
recall 0.00 is a respectable 0.50; the harmonic mean is 0.00. A model that
achieves a good score on one at the total expense of the other gets nothing,
which is exactly the behaviour you want from a summary of a rare class.

Macro-F1 then averages across classes:

$$
\text{macro-}F_1 = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K} F_1^{(k)}
$$

For the majority baseline: $F_1^{(\text{neg})} = 0$ and

$$
F_1^{(\text{pos})} = \frac{2 \cdot 0.9368 \cdot 1.0}{0.9368 + 1.0} = 0.9674,
$$

so macro-F1 $= (0 + 0.9674)/2 = 0.4837$.

**The analogy that makes this stick.** A hospital screening test for a
disease with 1-in-16 prevalence can achieve 93.7% "accuracy" by telling every
patient they are healthy. Accuracy weights each *patient* equally; macro-F1
weights each *class* equally. Which one you want is a question about
consequences, not about statistics — and for a review triage system where
the entire business value is catching the complaints, the negative class
carries the value, so it gets half the weight.

The same reasoning is why `class_weight="balanced"` appears in every model
below. It reweights the training loss by inverse class frequency, so one
negative review costs the optimiser about 14.8 times what one positive review
costs. Without it, every model in this chapter collapses toward the majority
class and the comparison measures nothing.
:::

From here on, **macro-F1 is the headline and accuracy is reported only to
show how misleading it is.** Watch the two columns diverge in every table
that follows.

## Tokenising Turkish, and the trap inside that

Before either road, the text has to become tokens. @sec-text-as-data made
lowercasing sound like the trivial step. In Turkish it is a bug.

```python
"IYI".lower()          # → 'iyi'
"İYİ".lower()          # → 'i̇yi̇'   (an i with an extra combining dot)
```

Turkish has two `i` letters — dotted `i`/`İ` and dotless `ı`/`I` — and they
are different letters, distinguishing different words. Python's default
`str.lower()` implements the English rule: `I` becomes `i`. In Turkish, `I`
must become `ı`, and `İ` must become `i`.

```python
TR_LOWER = str.maketrans({"I": "ı", "İ": "i"})
def tr_lower(s):
    return s.translate(TR_LOWER).lower()

tr_lower("IYI")        # → 'ıyı'
tr_lower("İYİ")        # → 'iyi'
```

```text
### the same string, two casefolding rules
             str.lower()      tr_lower()
"IYI"        iyi              ıyı
"İYİ"        i̇yi̇             iyi
```

The default rule silently merges `ıyı` into `iyi` and produces a
combining-dot hybrid for `İYİ` that matches nothing in your vocabulary. Both
are wrong; both fail quietly; both cost you accuracy you will attribute to
the model. **Casefolding is locale-dependent, and the locale is part of the
model.**

::: {.column-margin}
This class of bug is why the "just lowercase it" step in an English tutorial
is not portable advice. The equivalent traps elsewhere: German ß, Greek final
sigma, and any language where case is not a bijection.
:::

With that fixed, the tokeniser is a regex over the Turkish alphabet, and the
corpus looks like this:

```python
import re
TOKEN_RE = re.compile(r"[a-zçğıöşü]+")
def tokenize(s):
    return TOKEN_RE.findall(tr_lower(s))
```

```text
### the training corpus, 40,000 reviews
tokens                        903,190
distinct word forms            74,317
hapax (seen exactly once)      43,579     58.6% of all forms
mean review length               22.6 tokens
median                             19
95th percentile                    56
longest                           296
```

**58.6% of the vocabulary appears exactly once.** @sec-embeddings measured
50.0% on Turkish Wikipedia; user-generated review text is worse, because on
top of Turkish morphology you now have typos, and every typo is a new type.

The morphology is visible if you group word forms by their first five
characters:

```text
### distinct word forms sharing a five-character prefix
kulla    895 forms   kullanışlı, kullanıyorum, kullandım, kullanımı, kullanım, ...
bekle    285 forms   beklediğimden, beklediğim, beklemiyordum, beklemeyin, ...
çalış    247 forms   çalışıyor, çalışma, çalışan, çalışması, çalışırken, ...
çıkar    209 forms   çıkarıyor, çıkar, çıkartıyor, çıkarmıyor, çıkardı, ...
düşün    195 forms   düşünüyorum, düşünmeden, düşünenlere, düşünen, ...
```

::: {#gloss-bag-of-words .column-margin .term-gloss}
**bag-of-words** — count which words a document contains and forget the
order they came in. "Dog bites man" and "man bites dog" become the same
document. [↩](#term-bag-of-words){.term-back}
:::

Eight hundred and ninety-five distinct columns, in a [bag-of-words](#gloss-bag-of-words){#term-bag-of-words .term-ref} model, for
what a Turkish speaker experiences as one verb [@oflazer1994two]. Every one of
those columns is estimated separately, from its own handful of examples, and
nothing learned about `kullanışlı` transfers to `kullanıyorum`. That is
chapter 3's complaint, stated in the units of chapter 2, on real data.

Hold on to the number 895. The entire case for embeddings rests on it.

## Round 1 — the chapter-2 methods

Four counting schemes, all from @sec-text-as-data, all fed to the same
classifier.

```python
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer, TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

PAT = r"[a-zçğıöşü]+"
schemes = {
  "bag of words":    CountVectorizer(min_df=2, token_pattern=PAT),
  "tf-idf":          TfidfVectorizer(min_df=2, sublinear_tf=True, token_pattern=PAT),
  "tf-idf 1-2 gram": TfidfVectorizer(min_df=2, sublinear_tf=True,
                                     ngram_range=(1, 2), token_pattern=PAT),
  "tf-idf char 3-5": TfidfVectorizer(min_df=3, sublinear_tf=True,
                                     analyzer="char_wb", ngram_range=(3, 5)),
}
clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, class_weight="balanced", random_state=42)
```

```text
### round 1: counting
                      accuracy   macro-F1   F1(neg)   dims      fit
majority baseline        93.68      48.37      0.00      —        —
bag of words             92.14      73.51     51.30   30,195    0.7 s
tf-idf                   90.07      71.95     49.41   30,195    0.5 s
tf-idf 1-2 gram          92.57      76.21     56.47  101,659    1.0 s
tf-idf char_wb 3-5       88.63      70.39     47.14   94,939    3.3 s
```

Three things in that table are worth stopping for.

::: {#gloss-f1-score-macro-f1 .column-margin .term-gloss}
**F1 score / macro-F1** — one number that balances precision against
recall. *Macro* means it is worked out for each class and then averaged,
so a rare class counts as much as a common one. This is why it disagrees
with accuracy here. [↩](#term-f1-score-macro-f1){.term-back}
:::

**Accuracy and [macro-F1](#gloss-f1-score-macro-f1){#term-f1-score-macro-f1 .term-ref} rank the methods differently.** Bag-of-words has
*higher* accuracy than TF-IDF (92.14 vs 90.07) and *higher* macro-F1 (73.51 vs
71.95) — fine. But every counting method has *lower* accuracy than the
do-nothing baseline's 93.68, while scoring 22 to 28 macro-F1 points above it.
Any method that finds negatives at all must trade away some of the free
accuracy that ignoring them provided. If you optimise accuracy on this
dataset you will select the model that does nothing.

**Plain TF-IDF loses to plain counting here.** That is not what chapter 2's
narrative would lead you to expect, and the reason is the interaction between
IDF and short documents. Reviews average 22.6 tokens, most words appear once
in a document, so within-document term frequency carries almost no signal;
what IDF then does is down-weight exactly the frequent sentiment words —
`güzel`, `iyi`, `tavsiye` — that are the most reliable evidence available.
Rare words get amplified instead, and in a corpus that is 58.6% hapax, rare
mostly means *typo*.

::: {#gloss-bigram .column-margin .term-gloss}
**bigram** — a pair of words counted as a single unit, so that *not good*
can be told apart from *good*. [↩](#term-bigram){.term-back}
:::

**[Bigrams](#gloss-bigram){#term-bigram .term-ref} give the single largest gain in the chapter: +4.3 macro-F1.**
This is negation being captured, and it is worth seeing why. `değil` ("not")
as a unigram is a strong negative feature on its own, but `beğendim` ("I
liked it") and `beğenmedim` ("I did not like it") are already separate
unigrams thanks to Turkish morphology — the negation is a *suffix*, inside
the word. What bigrams add is the multi-word version: `tavsiye etmem`
("I do not recommend"), `memnun kalmadım` ("I was not satisfied"). Turkish
puts some negation in the morphology, where a bag of words gets it for free,
and some in the syntax, where it needs bigrams.

### What the model learned, in words

The under-rated property of a sparse linear model: the parameters are
readable. There is one coefficient per word, and you can simply sort them.

```text
### tf-idf + logistic regression, largest coefficients
towards POSITIVE                     towards NEGATIVE
gayet        +8.04  (quite)          etmiyorum    -8.16  (I do not [recommend])
ederim       +6.94  ([I] do)         değil        -6.95  (not)
mükemmel     +6.13  (perfect)        kötü         -6.63  (bad)
teşekkürler  +6.09  (thanks)         etmem        -6.35  (I would not)
harika       +5.93  (wonderful)      beğenmedim   -6.21  (I did not like it)
memnunum     +5.84  (I am pleased)   iade         -5.85  (return / refund)
güzel        +5.48  (nice)           fakat        -5.52  (however)
süper        +4.98  (super)          kalitesiz    -5.47  (low quality)
kaliteli     +4.32  (good quality)   kalmadım     -5.33  (I was not [satisfied])
```

Every one of those is defensible to a domain expert in a sentence, and two of
them are genuinely informative about the domain rather than about language:
`iade` ("refund") is a negative signal because people who return things are
unhappy, and `fakat`/`ama` ("however", "but") are negative because a Turkish
review that contains a contrastive conjunction is usually about to complain.
Nobody wrote those rules down. They fell out of 40,000 labels.

Keep this column in mind when the dense methods arrive, because none of them
can produce it.

## Round 2 — the chapter-3 methods

Now the same problem with coordinates. Three models from @sec-embeddings,
each trained from scratch on the 40,000 *training* documents only — no
pretrained vectors, no test text, no labels.

```python
from gensim.models import Word2Vec, FastText
from gensim.models.doc2vec import Doc2Vec, TaggedDocument

w2v = Word2Vec(train_tok, vector_size=100, window=5, min_count=2,
               sg=1, negative=5, epochs=10, workers=1, seed=42)
ft  = FastText(train_tok, vector_size=100, window=5, min_count=2,
               sg=1, negative=5, epochs=10, workers=1, seed=42,
               min_n=3, max_n=6, bucket=500_000)
d2v = Doc2Vec([TaggedDocument(d, [i]) for i, d in enumerate(train_tok)],
              vector_size=100, min_count=2, epochs=20, dm=0,
              negative=5, workers=1, seed=42)
```

A document vector is the mean of its word vectors, which is the standard
cheap answer from @sec-embeddings; doc2vec gets its vector directly.

```text
### round 2: coordinates
                      accuracy   macro-F1   F1(neg)   dims   embed train
averaged word2vec        79.92      61.39     34.64     100     14.7 s
averaged fastText        79.64      61.36     34.79     100     31.6 s
doc2vec (PV-DBOW)        71.96      55.13     27.66     100      8.5 s
```

Set against round 1:

```text
### both rounds, sorted by macro-F1
tf-idf 1-2 gram          92.57      76.21     56.47  101,659
bag of words             92.14      73.51     51.30   30,195
tf-idf                   90.07      71.95     49.41   30,195
tf-idf char_wb 3-5       88.63      70.39     47.14   94,939
averaged word2vec        79.92      61.39     34.64      100
averaged fastText        79.64      61.36     34.79      100
doc2vec (PV-DBOW)        71.96      55.13     27.66      100
majority baseline        93.68      48.37      0.00        —
```

::: {#gloss-recall .column-margin .term-gloss}
**recall** — of the reviews that really were negative, the share the model
found. It is the cost of a miss. [↩](#term-recall){.term-back}
:::

::: {#gloss-precision .column-margin .term-gloss}
**precision** — of the reviews the model called negative, the share that
really were. It is the cost of a false alarm. [↩](#term-precision){.term-back}
:::

**Counting wins, and not narrowly.** The gap between the best sparse method
and the best dense one is 14.8 macro-F1 points. On the negative class, where
the value is, it is 21.8 points of F1 — and the shape of that gap matters.
Averaged word2vec actually *finds* more negatives (84.2% [recall](#gloss-recall){#term-recall .term-ref} against
76.3%); it is simply wrong about them far more often, at 21.8% [precision](#gloss-precision){#term-precision .term-ref}
against 44.8%. Per complaint it flags, the sparse model is more than twice as
likely to be right.

This reproduces @sec-embeddings' 20 Newsgroups finding on a completely
different dataset, in a different language, with a different class structure
and seventeen times more training data. The ordering is not a quirk of one
benchmark. **For document classification with plenty of labels, averaged
static embeddings lose to counting.** Say it out loud now, because the rest of
the chapter is about the conditions under which it stops being true.

The one thing the dense methods win is size, and they win it enormously:
61.39 macro-F1 from **100 numbers per document** against 76.21 from 101,659
dimensions. Measured against that best-scoring sparse model, which needs
word *and* character n-grams to get there, it is a 1,017-fold compression
for a 19% relative loss; measured against plain word tf-idf and its 30,195
columns it is 302-fold, which is the figure in the summary table later in
this chapter. If you are running nearest-neighbour search over ten million
documents, that ratio is your entire architecture. If you are fitting a
linear model on 40,000 documents, it buys you nothing at all, because a
sparse matrix with 19.8 non-zeros per row was never the bottleneck.

::: {.column-margin}
Note the direction of the dense models' errors: averaged word2vec recalls
84.2% of negatives — *better* than any sparse model — at 21.8% precision. It
is not blind to the minority class; it is imprecise about it. The blur is in
the representation, and `class_weight="balanced"` converts that blur into
false alarms rather than misses.
:::

## The out-of-vocabulary test

Chapter 3 made a specific promise about Turkish, one that could be proved
wrong: word2vec breaks
on unseen word forms, fastText does not. Here is the measurement on the test
set.

```text
### coverage of the 10,000 test reviews
test tokens                     229,055
outside the word2vec vocabulary  16,660     7.27% of tokens
distinct test word forms         32,573
outside the vocabulary           15,098     46.4% of forms
test reviews with no usable token     7
```

Chapter 3 predicted 7.33% on Wikipedia; reviews give 7.27%. The prediction
holds almost exactly. But look at the second pair of numbers, because they
are the ones that hurt: **46.4% of the distinct word forms in the test set
were never seen in training.** Nearly half the vocabulary of any new batch of
reviews is, to word2vec, a `KeyError`.

fastText's coverage of that same set is 100%, by construction — it sums
character n-gram vectors, so any string of characters gets a vector. Here is
what those vectors are like for word forms that are genuinely absent from
training:

```text
### nearest neighbours for unseen word forms
kargolanmamış  ("not having been shipped")
  word2vec   KeyError
  fastText   kargolanmış, kargolandı, kargolanma, kargolanıp, kargolu

tavsiyelerim  ("my recommendations")
  word2vec   KeyError
  fastText   tavsiyeleri, tavsiyeler, tavsiyeederim, tavsiyedir

hızlıcana  (colloquial "nice and fast")
  word2vec   KeyError
  fastText   hızlıca, hızlıda, hızlısı, hızlıydı, hızlı
```

That is a clean win, exactly as advertised [@bojanowski2017enriching]. Every
unseen form lands next to its own stem family.

Now the finding that makes this chapter worth writing. Compare the two models
on words that are *in* both vocabularies:

```text
### nearest neighbours for a common word
kargo  ("shipping")
  word2vec   teslimat, gönderim, gönderi, kargoda, kargoyla, kargolama
             (delivery, dispatch, shipment — different words, same topic)
  fastText   kargocu, kargolu, kargosu, kargonuz, kargom, kargomun
             (courier, with-shipping, its-shipping, your-shipping, my-shipping)

kalitesiz  ("low quality")
  word2vec   dandik, kullanışsız, dayanıksız, uyduruk, kırılacak
             (shoddy, unusable, flimsy, fake, about-to-break)
  fastText   kalitesizmiş, kalitesizliği, kalitel, kalitesi, kalitesindeki
             (…all forms of the same stem, including "kalitesi" = quality)
```

**word2vec's neighbours are semantic. fastText's are orthographic.** Asked
what is like `kalitesiz` ("low quality"), word2vec answers with five other
ways to say a product is bad. fastText answers with the word `kalitesi`
("its quality") — which is not a synonym, it is the *opposite* polarity
sharing six leading characters.

This is @sec-embeddings' stated weakness — *assumes spelling similarity
implies meaning similarity* — showing up as a measurable cost. The subword
budget that buys perfect coverage is spent on modelling morphology, and it is
taken from the budget that was modelling meaning.

Which is why, having solved the out-of-vocabulary problem completely,
fastText scores **61.36** where word2vec scores **61.39**. The fix worked
perfectly and bought nothing.

::: {.fig-cap}
The out-of-vocabulary problem is real, fastText solves it completely, and on
this task solving it changes nothing. Coverage is a property of the
representation; accuracy is a property of the representation *and the task*.
An [intrinsic](#gloss-intrinsic-extrinsic-evaluation){#term-intrinsic-extrinsic-evaluation .term-ref} fix only pays if the thing it fixed was what the task was
limited by — here, it was not.
:::
::::

::: {#gloss-intrinsic-extrinsic-evaluation .column-margin .term-gloss}
**intrinsic / extrinsic evaluation** — *intrinsic* scores the
representation on its own terms, such as how many words it covers.
*Extrinsic* scores it on the job you actually need doing. This chapter is
a long argument that only the second one settles anything. [↩](#term-intrinsic-extrinsic-evaluation){.term-back}
:::

One more diagnostic, because it corrects a natural misreading. Being *in*
the vocabulary is not the same as being *well estimated*:

```text
### kalitesizmiş — in the word2vec vocabulary, seen a handful of times
  word2vec   ayakkabıların, kaymak, yapışır, temizlenmemiş, zorlamadım
             (of the shoes, cream, it sticks, uncleaned, I did not force)
  fastText   kalitesiz, kalitesizliği, kalitesinide, kalitesi
```

word2vec has a vector for this word and the vector is noise. The 46.4%
out-of-vocabulary rate is therefore an *understatement* of the problem: past
the vocabulary boundary you get an error, which is at least honest, but just
inside it you get confident nonsense.

## Why the dense methods lost

Two representations, 84.1% agreement on the test set. Where they disagree,
TF-IDF is right 1,315 times and averaged fastText is right 272 — nearly five
to one. The interesting question is what the 272 look like.

```text
### averaged fastText right, tf-idf wrong        (gold: positive)
  "en guvenli alısveriş sitesi"        no diacritics at all
  "çok hizli ve temi̇z tesli̇mat"        broken diacritics mid-word
  "çok sessiz çalışıyor makina ."      "makina" — colloquial for "makine"

### tf-idf right, averaged fastText wrong
  "sıkıcı edebi yonu cok zayif"        gold negative — ft says positive
  "koku ne çok kötü ne çok iyi"        gold negative — "neither… nor…"
  "cok guzel! kedi bayildi buna"       gold positive — ft says negative
```

The dense wins are exactly the promised ones: misspellings and missing
diacritics, where a count vector sees an unknown column and a subword model
sees a familiar shape. The dense losses are the promised ones too — the
second example is a `ne … ne …` construction ("neither very bad nor very
good") in which every individual word is positive and the *structure* carries
the negation.

That points at the real cause, and it is testable directly.

```text
### cosine between a review and its negation
                                                  averaged     tf-idf
                                                   fastText
ürünü çok beğendim / ürünü hiç beğenmedim            0.776       0.193
kesinlikle tavsiye ederim / … tavsiye etmem          0.919       0.474
kargo çok hızlı geldi / kargo çok yavaş geldi        0.943       0.572
fiyatına göre gayet kaliteli / … hiç kaliteli değil  0.892       0.690
bu üründen memnun kaldım / … memnun kalmadım         0.962       0.582
```

Averaging places a sentence and its opposite at cosine 0.78–0.96. TF-IDF
places the same pairs at 0.19–0.69. The mean of a handful of vectors is
dominated by the words the two sentences share, and in a negated pair that is
almost all of them — the one word carrying the reversal is averaged into
nothing along with everything else.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The arithmetic of why averaging dilutes negation

Take a five-word review and its negation, differing in exactly one word:

$$
\mathbf{d}_+ = \frac{1}{5}\left(\mathbf{v}_1 + \mathbf{v}_2 + \mathbf{v}_3 + \mathbf{v}_4 + \mathbf{v}_{\text{liked}}\right), \qquad
\mathbf{d}_- = \frac{1}{5}\left(\mathbf{v}_1 + \mathbf{v}_2 + \mathbf{v}_3 + \mathbf{v}_4 + \mathbf{v}_{\text{disliked}}\right)
$$

The difference is

$$
\mathbf{d}_+ - \mathbf{d}_- = \frac{1}{5}\left(\mathbf{v}_{\text{liked}} - \mathbf{v}_{\text{disliked}}\right),
$$

so the entire semantic reversal survives at **one fifth strength**, while the
four shared words contribute their full magnitude to both vectors and push the
cosine towards 1. Lengthen the review to twenty words and the reversal is at
one twentieth. *The longer the review, the more completely averaging erases
the word that changed its meaning.*

Worse, in a subword model $\mathbf{v}_{\text{liked}}$ and
$\mathbf{v}_{\text{disliked}}$ are not even far apart, because `beğendim` and
`beğenmedim` share the n-grams `beğ`, `eğe`, `ğen`. fastText's own mechanism
pulls the numerator towards zero.

TF-IDF has the opposite structure. `beğendim` and `beğenmedim` are two
distinct columns; a document containing one has a hard zero in the other. No
dilution is possible because there is no averaging — which is precisely why
its cosines land at 0.19 rather than 0.78.

**The analogy.** Averaging word vectors is taking the mean colour of a
painting. Two paintings that differ only in that one is a sunrise and the
other a sunset have nearly the same mean colour, and the mean colour is the
only thing your classifier gets to see. A bag of words is instead a list of
which pigments appear — rougher about relationships, but it never loses the
one pigment that changed.
:::

Note what the classifier still manages in spite of this. Averaged fastText
assigns "ürünü çok beğendim" probability 0.82 of being positive and its
negation 0.02 — it gets the sign right even at cosine 0.776, because logistic
regression can find a direction in which the residual one-fifth is
discriminative. Watering the signal down is not the same as deleting it.
But it is a much harder problem handed to a linear model, and the
14.8-point gap is what it costs.

## The crossover: when embeddings do win

Everything so far has compared methods with 40,000 labelled reviews. That is
a luxury. The question that actually decides representation choice in
practice is: *how many labels do you have?*

The embedding models were trained without labels — they read the raw text and
learned from co-occurrence alone. That knowledge is already paid for before
the first review is annotated. TF-IDF has no such head start: its axes are
just words, and everything it knows about sentiment must come out of the
labelled set.

So hold the representations fixed and vary only the number of labels the
classifier sees.

```text
### macro-F1 by labelled training size (same test set of 10,000)
    n     negatives   tf-idf   tf-idf char   word2vec   fastText
   100        6        48.37       48.37       53.51      53.87
   250       16        48.53       48.84       61.59      63.10
   500       32        49.28       50.60       61.02      61.16
 1,000       63        55.40       58.55       59.52      59.93
 2,500      158        66.61       68.36       60.91      61.19
 5,000      316        71.16       70.47       61.52      60.80
10,000      632        72.55       71.29       61.80      61.56
20,000    1,264        72.42       71.26       60.94      60.96
40,000    2,529        71.95       70.39       61.39      61.36
```


::: {.fig-cap}
Four representations, nine training sizes, the same test set throughout; the
only variable is how much labelled data the classifier is given. At 250
labels the embedding
models are 14.6 macro-F1 points *ahead*; at 40,000 they are 10.6 points
behind. Both of chapter 2's and chapter 3's claims are true — they are true
in different regimes, and the regime is set by your annotation budget.
:::
::::

Read the left edge of that chart carefully. **With 250 labelled reviews — of
which 16 are negative — TF-IDF scores 48.53, which is the do-nothing
baseline.** It has learned nothing whatsoever. Averaged fastText scores 63.10
with the same 250 labels, which is better than TF-IDF manages with 1,000.

The reason is the mechanism, not luck. With 16 negative examples, TF-IDF sees
16 sparse rows drawn from a 30,195-dimensional space; a word that appeared in
one of them and nowhere else gets a large coefficient supported by a single
observation, and the model generalises to nothing. The embedding model was
trained on all 903,190 tokens of unlabelled text before any label existed, so
it already knows that `kalitesiz`, `dandik` and `dayanıksız` occupy the same
region. Sixteen labels is enough to learn *which side of a boundary that
region falls on* — one decision in 100 dimensions instead of thirty thousand.

::: {.column-margin}
This is the general principle behind every pretrained model in this book,
visible in miniature. Self-supervised training converts unlabelled text into a
representation in which the supervised problem is low-dimensional. The
embeddings do not know about sentiment; they know about Turkish, and knowing
about Turkish is most of the work when you have sixteen examples.
:::

And then the curve flattens. Averaged fastText is at 61.16 with 500 labels
and 61.36 with 40,000 — **eighty times the supervision for two tenths of a
point.** The information bottleneck is no longer the labels, it is the
representation: once you have averaged a review into 100 numbers, the
distinction between "the shipping was fast" and "the shipping was slow" is
partly gone, and no quantity of labels restores it. TF-IDF, meanwhile, keeps
climbing until about 10,000 labels because each new label can sharpen an
individual word's coefficient.

**Two curves, two different limits: embeddings are limited by their
representation, counts are limited by their labels.** That sentence is the
practical content of this chapter, and it generalises well past these seven
methods.

## What it costs

Accuracy is not the only axis. Here is the whole bill.

```text
### cost, on one CPU core, 40,000 training documents
                      build the        vectorise      training
                      representation   10,000 test    matrix
tf-idf                     0.5 s          0.11 s        9.7 MB
tf-idf 1-2 gram            0.9 s          0.17 s       15.4 MB
tf-idf char_wb 3-5         2.9 s          0.72 s      144.8 MB
word2vec + averaging      14.7 s          0.11 s       16.0 MB
fastText + averaging      31.6 s          0.27 s       16.0 MB
doc2vec                    8.5 s          1.73 s       16.0 MB
```

Two entries deserve comment.

**Character n-grams are expensive out of proportion to their benefit.** 144.8
MB and 301 non-zeros per document, for 70.39 macro-F1 — worse than plain
bag-of-words at 9.7 MB. They are the right tool when spelling is the problem
(and they were the *best* sparse method at 1,000 labels, where they beat word
TF-IDF by 3.2 points), but they are not a free upgrade.

**doc2vec must run gradient descent to vectorise a new document.** 1.73
seconds for 10,000 reviews, against 0.11 for averaging — a 16-fold difference,
and unlike training it is paid on every request, forever. Combined with the
worst macro-F1 in the comparison (55.13), this is the clearest
recommendation in the chapter: for classification, **do not use doc2vec.**
@sec-embeddings had it ahead of averaging on 20 Newsgroups; on 40,000 short,
noisy Turkish reviews it is 6.3 points behind. Long, clean documents are the
regime where learning a document vector pays, and reviews are neither.

### The hybrid, and an honest negative result

The obvious move is to concatenate: character TF-IDF for spelling robustness,
averaged fastText for semantics, one classifier over both.

```text
### tf-idf char_wb 3-5  ⊕  averaged fastText   (95,039 dimensions)
accuracy   89.36     macro-F1   71.65     F1(neg)   49.24
```

It beats both of its parts — char TF-IDF alone scored 70.39, fastText alone
61.36 — and it loses to plain word bigrams by 4.6 points while taking 6.2
seconds to fit against the bigram model's 0.1. Concatenation is a real
technique and this is a real
gain over the components, but it did not rescue the dense representation, and
reporting it as a success by comparing only against its parts would be
exactly the kind of selective baseline this chapter is arguing against.

## Choosing, on purpose

| | [Strengths]{.pro} | [Weaknesses]{.con} | Choose it when |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Bag of words** | Fastest to build and reason about. Beat TF-IDF here on short documents. Coefficients readable word by word. | No length normalisation; long documents dominate. No notion of which words are informative. | You want a baseline in five minutes that is genuinely hard to beat, and your documents are short. |
| **TF-IDF (words)** | The standard strong baseline. Down-weights ubiquitous words. Trivially interpretable and auditable. | [Hurt]{.con} by IDF on short texts — lost to raw counts here. One column per word form: 895 columns for one Turkish verb. Zero generalisation to unseen forms. | Documents are long enough for term frequency to mean something, and you have thousands of labels. |
| **TF-IDF (word bigrams)** | Best score in this chapter, 76.21. Captures multi-word negation that unigrams miss. Still a linear model you can read. | 3.4× the columns. Gains shrink as documents get longer. Still blind to unseen vocabulary. | You have labels and the task turns on short phrases — sentiment, intent, triage. This should be your default. |
| **TF-IDF (char n-grams)** | Immune to spelling: no vocabulary to fall outside of. Strongest sparse method in the low-label regime. Language-agnostic — no tokeniser to get wrong. | 144.8 MB and 301 non-zeros per document. Lower macro-F1 than plain counting at full data. Coefficients are not human-readable. | Spelling is unreliable, the language is agglutinative, or you have no trustworthy tokeniser. |
| **Averaged word2vec** | 100 dimensions for 61.4 macro-F1 — 302× fewer dimensions than word tf-idf. Trained without labels. [Ahead of every sparse method]{.pro} under ~1,500 labels. Semantic neighbours you can inspect. | `KeyError` on 46.4% of unseen word forms. Confident nonsense on rare in-vocabulary words. Averaging dilutes negation. Word order gone. | Labels are scarce, or you need compact vectors for similarity search over millions of documents. |
| **Averaged fastText** | Every string gets a vector — coverage is 100% by construction. Handles the missing diacritics and typos in real user text. Best of any method at 250 labels. | Neighbours are [orthographic, not semantic]{.con}: `kalitesiz` → `kalitesi`. 2× word2vec's training time. Bought perfect coverage for +0.0 macro-F1 here. | The text is user-generated and misspelled, the language is agglutinative, and you cannot control the input vocabulary. |
| **doc2vec** | One vector per document with no averaging heuristic. Learns document-level structure averaging cannot. | [Worst]{.con} score here, 55.13. Inference needs gradient steps: 16× slower per document, forever. Extra hyperparameters. | Documents are long and clean and you have measured that it beats averaging on *your* data. Rarely, on short text. |

: What to reach for, and why {tbl-colwidths="[13,30,30,27]"}

The decision procedure, compressed to something you can apply before writing
any code:

```text
### how to choose, in order
1. Count your labels.
     < ~1,500 → averaged embeddings (fastText if morphology or typos)
     > ~1,500 → sparse counts, and start with word bigrams
2. Check your document length.
     short (< 50 tokens) → raw counts may beat tf-idf; test both, it is free
     long                → tf-idf, and doc2vec becomes worth testing
3. Check your vocabulary stability.
     users type it → character n-grams or subwords
     you control it → word features are fine
4. Check what you must ship.
     an explanation → sparse, always
     10M vectors for similarity search → dense, always
5. Only now consider anything more complicated.
```

## The failure they share

It would be a poor summary to leave you with "counting won". Both families
fail in the same place, and the failure is the reason there is a Part II.

```text
### two reviews, same words, opposite meaning
a = "kalite iyi fiyat kötü"      (quality good, price bad)
b = "kalite kötü fiyat iyi"      (quality bad, price good)

cosine, averaged fastText   1.0000
cosine, tf-idf              1.0000
```

Not approximately equal. **Identical**, to every decimal place either
representation can produce. TF-IDF sees the same four words with the same
counts. Averaging sees the same four vectors summed in a different order, and
addition is commutative. Neither representation contains the information that
would distinguish a complaint about price from a complaint about quality,
so no classifier built on top of them can ever recover it — not with more
labels, not with a better classifier, not ever.

For sentiment on product reviews this rarely bites, because most reviews are
entirely positive or entirely negative and the bag is sufficient. For
"which component is the customer complaining about", it is fatal.

Every method in this chapter is a function from a *set* of words to a vector.
To distinguish those two sentences the representation has to be a function of
the *sequence*: something that reads `kalite`, then `iyi`, and produces a
different state than if it had read `kalite`, then `kötü`. That is a language
model, and it is @sec-language-models. Making that state depend on every
other word at once is attention, and it is @sec-transformers.

The bake-off has told us exactly what to demand of them: keep TF-IDF's
sensitivity to the individual decisive word, keep embeddings' generalisation
across word forms and their tiny label appetite, and add the one thing
neither has — order.

## Intuition checks

Answer before expanding.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Your client has 400 labelled support tickets in Turkish and 2 million unlabelled ones. Which representation?

Averaged fastText, and the second sentence of the question is why.

At 400 labels you are on the left of the crossover chart, where TF-IDF is
still near the do-nothing baseline — at 500 labels it scored 49.28 against
fastText's 61.16. Two million unlabelled tickets is a large free corpus for
self-supervised training, and it is exactly the resource an embedding model
converts into performance and a count model cannot use at all.

Choose fastText over word2vec because the tickets are Turkish and
user-written: 46.4% of unseen word forms were out of vocabulary here, and
support tickets are worse than reviews.

Then say the second half out loud: *label 2,000 more tickets and re-run this
comparison*, because the chart says the answer flips.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. A colleague reports 93% accuracy and wants to ship. What do you ask for?

The confusion matrix, and then the macro-F1.

93% is below the 93.68% you get by predicting the majority class for every
input, so on this dataset that model may be worse than a constant. The two
follow-up questions: how many of the 632 negatives did it find, and what
happens downstream to the ones it missed?

The general form of the question is *what is the accuracy of the trivial
baseline* — and you should ask it before you look at any reported score, not
after.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. fastText fixed the out-of-vocabulary problem completely. Why did the score not move?

Because out-of-vocabulary was not the binding constraint.

Coverage went from 53.6% of word forms to 100%, and macro-F1 went from 61.39
to 61.36. The two dense models are both limited by *averaging*, not by
lookup: they place a sentence and its negation at cosine 0.78–0.96, and no
improvement in the word vectors changes that, because the damage is done by
the mean.

There is also a cost hiding in the fix. fastText spends its capacity on
character n-grams, so its nearest neighbours become morphological rather than
semantic — `kalitesiz` retrieves `kalitesi`, which has the opposite polarity.
It gained coverage and lost some meaning, and the two roughly cancelled.

The transferable lesson: an intrinsic improvement only shows up extrinsically
if the thing it improved was the bottleneck. Measure which one you have
before you fix either.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. Would 300-dimensional vectors, or pretrained ones, have changed the verdict?

They would move the numbers and not the shape.

Larger vectors and pretrained Turkish embeddings [@mikolov2018advances] would
lift the dense curve — probably a few points, and more at the left edge
where extra pretraining data matters most. What they cannot do is fix
averaging: the negation cosines and the exactly-1.0000 word-order result are
properties of the mean, not of the vectors being meant. The crossover would
shift right; it would not disappear.

The honest way to settle it is @sec-embeddings' exercise 6, which is now well
specified: rerun this chapter's script with 300-dimensional pretrained
vectors and report whether the crossover moves past your actual label budget.
That is the only version of the question that affects a decision.
:::

## Interview questions {#sec-bake-off-interview}

Representation choice is the most common design question in an applied NLP
screen, and the most common wrong answer is to name the newest method. Every
answer below is one this chapter measured, so you can quote a number instead of
a preference.

::: {.column-margin}
The pattern in all five: name the axis the question is really about — labels,
morphology, structure, cost — then give the measurement, then say what would
change your answer. An answer with no number is an opinion; an answer with no
*condition* is a slogan.
:::

1. **Embeddings or TF-IDF for text classification?** Ask how many labels they
   have, because that is the axis the answer turns on. On this corpus the
   curves cross at roughly **1,500 labels**: at 250 labels averaged fastText
   scores 63.10 macro-F1 against TF-IDF's 48.84 — which is the do-nothing
   baseline — and at 40,000 TF-IDF scores 76.21 against 61.36. The embeddings
   were trained without labels, so their knowledge is paid for before the first
   annotation; TF-IDF has to buy everything it knows out of the labelled set.
   Finish with the shape: [the dense curve plateaus and the sparse one keeps
   climbing]{.hl}, so the more labels you expect to get, the more the answer
   tilts sparse.

2. **Why would averaging word vectors lose to counting words?** Because
   averaging destroys the thing sentiment lives in. Measured directly: a review
   and its negation sit at cosine **0.78 to 0.96** under averaged fastText and
   **0.19 to 0.69** under TF-IDF. The mean of a handful of vectors is dominated
   by the words the two sentences *share*, and in a negated pair that is nearly
   all of them — the one word carrying the reversal is averaged into nothing.
   The good version of this answer names the fix as well: weighted averaging
   with the first principal component removed [@arora2017simple] is the
   cheapest thing to try before reaching for an encoder.

3. **Turkish is morphologically rich. Which method does that argue for?**
   fastText over word2vec, and the number to quote is not the token rate. On
   this test set 7.27% of *tokens* were outside the word2vec vocabulary, which
   sounds survivable — but **46.4% of the distinct word forms** were, so nearly
   half the vocabulary of any new batch is a `KeyError`. fastText covers 100% by
   construction because it sums character n-grams. Then deliver the twist,
   because it is the part that shows you measured rather than assumed:
   [fixing out-of-vocabulary coverage completely moved macro-F1 by 0.03
   points]{.hl}, 61.39 to 61.36. Coverage was never the bottleneck; averaging
   was.

4. **How would you pick between two representations that score within a point
   of each other?** Stop looking at the aggregate and cross-tabulate. These two
   agree on 84.1% of the test set; where they disagree TF-IDF is right 1,315
   times and averaged fastText 272 — nearly five to one, which is a much
   sharper signal than the headline gap. Then read the 272: they are missing
   diacritics and colloquial spellings, exactly what a subword model should
   win. That tells you the two are complementary, which is a different decision
   from "one is better".

5. **What does the cheap method cost, and does that matter?** Have the numbers.
   TF-IDF 1-2 gram: 0.9 s to build, 0.17 s to vectorise 10,000 documents,
   15.4 MB. fastText: 31.6 s to train, 16.0 MB. Both are trivial, which is the
   point — [at this scale the cost axis does not decide anything, so do not
   pretend it does]{.hl}. Say that plainly. Cost becomes the deciding axis at
   the scale of @sec-classification-crossover, where a prompted model costs 142×
   more per document than a fine-tuned encoder, and knowing *when* an axis
   starts mattering is the skill being tested.

6. **Everything here is beaten by a fine-tuned encoder. Why learn it?** Two
   reasons, and the second is the real one. First, the crossover is real:
   below roughly 1,000 labels the encoder in @sec-classification-finetune is
   worse than both methods in this chapter. Second, this chapter is where the
   *diagnostic* habits come from — the negation-cosine probe, the
   disagreement cross-tabulation, the coverage-versus-score distinction. Those
   transfer to every model you will ever ship. A candidate who can only run
   `AutoModel.from_pretrained` cannot tell you why their model fails.

## Where to go deeper

- **fastText for classification** [@joulin2017bag]. A linear model over
  averaged subword n-grams, trained in minutes on a CPU, reported as "on par
  with deep learning classifiers". The direct industrial ancestor of this
  chapter's round 2, and still an excellent production answer for
  high-volume, low-latency routing.
- **Enriching word vectors with subword information**
  [@bojanowski2017enriching]. The paper behind the coverage result above,
  with the morphologically rich languages — Turkish included — where it
  helps most.
- **Distributed representations of sentences and documents**
  [@le2014distributed]. doc2vec's original claims, worth reading against this
  chapter's measurement of it.
- **A simple but tough-to-beat baseline for sentence embeddings**
  [@arora2017simple]. Weighted averaging with the first principal component
  removed — the cheapest realistic upgrade to round 2, and the first thing to
  try if you want to move the dense curve.
- **scikit-learn** [@pedregosa2011scikit] and **gensim**
  [@rehurek2010software]. The two libraries this chapter is built from; the
  user guides are unusually good.

## Exercises

1. **Move the crossover.** Rerun the learning curve with `min_df=1` and with
   `min_df=5` for TF-IDF. Predict first which direction the low-label end
   moves, then check. Explain the result in terms of how many observations
   support each coefficient.
2. **Kill the imbalance instead.** Drop `class_weight="balanced"` and rerun
   every model. Report accuracy *and* macro-F1 for each. Which methods
   collapse to the majority class, and why does the ranking by accuracy
   change more than the ranking by macro-F1?
3. **Weighted averaging.** Implement @arora2017simple: average the word
   vectors with weight $a/(a + p(w))$ for $a = 10^{-3}$, then remove the
   first principal component of the resulting document matrix. Report the
   new dense scores. Did it beat plain averaging, and did it close any of
   the 14.8-point gap?
4. **The negation probe, extended.** Build twenty negation pairs from your
   own domain and measure both cosines. Then find the pair with the highest
   averaged-embedding cosine that the classifier *still* gets right, and
   explain how it can.
5. **Break the char n-gram model.** Character n-grams were the best sparse
   method at 1,000 labels and among the worst at 40,000. Construct the
   argument for why, using the number of features and the number of
   observations per feature, then test it by varying `min_df`.
6. **A different task, same pipeline.** Swap sentiment for a task where the
   bag is insufficient — for example, labelling which aspect (shipping,
   price, quality) a review complains about. Predict what happens to the gap
   between counting and embeddings before you run it, then run it.
7. **Reproduce the casefolding bug.** Run the whole round-1 table with
   `str.lower()` instead of `tr_lower()` and report the damage in macro-F1.
   Then estimate how many test tokens were affected, and check whether the
   damage is proportional.
8. **Ship one.** Take the winning configuration, write the confusion matrix
   at three different decision thresholds, and choose one — writing the
   sentence that justifies the choice to whoever handles the false alarms.
   That sentence, not the macro-F1, is the actual deliverable.
